title: How Foreign RSUs Are Taxed in India (FY 2026-27): Vesting, Sale, Schedule FA and FTC
summary: RSUs from a foreign employer are taxed as salary when they vest and as capital gains when you sell. Rates, the exchange rate rule, reporting and a worked example.
body_markdown:
If your employer is listed abroad and part of your pay arrives as RSUs, India taxes those shares at two points. The value of the shares is taxed as salary when they vest, and any gain after that is taxed as capital gains when you sell.


Your employer handles only the first of these, and often only part of it. Advance tax, dividends, capital gains and foreign asset reporting are all yours to manage.


This guide covers each stage for FY 2026-27 (Tax Year 2026-27), the first year under the Income-tax Act, 2025. It follows one example, Priya, from vesting through to sale.

## The two taxable events


**Vesting.** The fair market value (FMV) of the shares that vest is a perquisite. It is added to your salary for the year and taxed at your slab rate, whether or not you sell.


**Sale.** When you sell, the difference between the sale value and the value already taxed at vesting is a capital gain or loss.


Everything else in this guide is detail on these two events, plus the reporting that sits around them.


## Do I get taxed twice on RSUs?


No. Salary tax at vesting and capital gains tax at sale fall on two different amounts. The value taxed at vesting becomes your cost of acquisition, so only the gain after vesting is taxed when you sell.


It can still feel like double tax because both events come from the same shares, and because the first one arrives before you have received any cash. If the share price falls after vesting, you book a capital loss on sale. The salary tax you paid at vesting is not refunded.


## At grant: nothing is taxed


A grant is a promise of shares in the future. You do not own anything yet, so there is no income, no tax and nothing to report in your return.


Unvested units also stay out of Schedule FA. Only shares that have vested and been delivered to you are foreign assets.


## At vesting: taxed as salary


On the vesting date, the shares become yours. Their FMV is a perquisite under section 17(1)(d) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 17(2)(vi) of the 1961 Act) and forms part of your salary income.


### 1. How the perquisite is valued


For shares listed on a foreign exchange, the FMV per share in foreign currency is converted into rupees. Under[Rule 206](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/rule-206-1) of the Income-tax Rules, 2026, salary income in foreign currency is converted at the SBI telegraphic transfer buying rate (TTBR) on the last day of the month before the month in which it becomes due.


So for a July vest, the rate is SBI's TTBR for 30 June.


**Perquisite (INR) = shares vested × FMV per share × SBI TTBR on the last day of the previous month**


For how the FMV itself is determined, read[fair market value of RSUs explained](https://paasa.com/blog/fair-market-value-rsu-explained) .


### 2. How the tax is collected


Your employer must deduct TDS on the perquisite under section 392 (section 192 of the 1961 Act), like on the rest of your salary. Most employers do this through sell-to-cover: a portion of the vested shares is sold and the proceeds go towards the tax.


The perquisite and the TDS both show up in your Form 130 (the new number for Form 16) and Form 123 (earlier Form 12BA). Read[how to read Form 16 if you receive RSUs](https://paasa.com/blog/form-16-rsu-holders) to check them.


**Note:** You are taxed on all the shares that vest, including the ones sold to cover tax. The shares sold under sell-to-cover also produce a small capital gain or loss of their own, which you report in your return.


### 3. Your cost of acquisition is fixed here


The rupee value taxed as a perquisite becomes the cost of acquisition of the shares under section 73(1) (section 49(2AA) of the 1961 Act). It is fixed in rupees on the vesting date and does not move with the exchange rate afterwards.


**Example.** Suppose you are Priya, an engineering manager in Bengaluru whose total income falls between ₹50 lakh and ₹1 crore. On 14 July 2026, 100 shares of your US-listed employer vest at an FMV of $180 per share. Take SBI's TTBR for 30 June 2026 as ₹94.00 (an illustrative rate, close to where it stood then). Your employer uses sell-to-cover.


Item Amount


Shares vested 100


FMV per share $180


SBI TTBR for 30 June 2026 (illustrative) ₹94.00


Perquisite added to salary (100 × $180 × ₹94.00) ₹16,92,000


Income tax at 30% ₹5,07,600


Surcharge at 10% ₹50,760


Health and education cess at 4% ₹22,334


**Total tax on the vest** **₹5,80,694**


Shares sold to cover the tax (at ₹16,920 per share) 35


**Shares delivered to Priya** **65**


### The result: ₹5.81 lakh of tax, paid by selling 35 of the 100 shares


The tax works out to a little over 34 shares, so 35 are sold and the small excess is adjusted through payroll. Priya is taxed on all 100 shares but receives 65.


Her cost of acquisition is ₹16,920 per share, which comes to ₹10,99,800 for the 65 shares she holds.


## How much tax will I pay on RSUs?


At vesting, you pay your marginal salary rate on the full value of the shares. For most RSU holders that is the 30% slab plus surcharge and cess. In Priya's case it works out to 34.32% of the vest value.


Total income Surcharge Effective rate on the vest (30% slab)


Up to ₹50 lakh Nil 31.2%


₹50 lakh to ₹1 crore 10% 34.32%


₹1 crore to ₹2 crore 15% 35.88%


Above ₹2 crore (new regime) 25% 39%


At sale, you pay tax only on the gain after vesting: your slab rate if you held the shares for 24 months or less, and 12.5% if you held them for more than 24 months, plus surcharge and cess in both cases.


A large vest can push your income into a higher surcharge band, which raises the rate on your entire income and not just the RSUs. Read[the RSU surcharge problem between ₹50 lakh and ₹1 crore](https://paasa.com/blog/rsu-surcharge-problem-50l-1cr) for how that works. For a lot-by-lot calculation, use our[step-by-step RSU tax calculation guide](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-calculate-rsu-taxes-india) .


## At sale: taxed as capital gains


Selling vested shares is the second taxable event. No tax is deducted at source in India on this sale, so you compute and pay it yourself.


### 1. Holding period and rate


Shares listed only on a foreign exchange are treated like unlisted shares for Indian tax purposes. The holding period runs from the vesting date to the sale date.


Holding period from vesting Classification Tax rate


24 months or less Short-term capital gain Your slab rate


More than 24 months Long-term capital gain 12.5% without indexation (section 197)


The ₹1.25 lakh long-term exemption applies only to Indian listed equity on which securities transaction tax is paid. It does not apply to foreign shares.


### 2. Converting the sale into rupees


Your cost is already fixed in rupees from the vesting date. The sale proceeds are converted at SBI's TTBR on the last day of the month before the month of sale, under Rule 206.


**Capital gain (INR) = sale value in INR − cost of acquisition in INR**


**Example.** Suppose Priya sells her 65 shares on 21 August 2028 at $230 per share. She has held them for more than 24 months, so the gain is long-term. That date is in the future, so assume SBI's TTBR for 31 July 2028 is ₹96.00 and her income is still between ₹50 lakh and ₹1 crore.


Item Amount


Sale value (65 × $230 × ₹96.00) ₹14,35,200


Cost of acquisition (65 × ₹16,920, fixed at vesting) ₹10,99,800


Long-term capital gain ₹3,35,400


Tax at 12.5% ₹41,925


Surcharge at 10% ₹4,193


Health and education cess at 4% ₹1,845


**Total tax on the sale** **₹47,963**


### The result: about ₹48,000 of tax on a ₹3.35 lakh gain


Had Priya sold in 24 months or less, the same gain would have been taxed at her slab rate, or about ₹1.15 lakh. For set-off rules, loss carry-forward and the sell-to-cover lot, read[capital gains tax on RSU shares](https://paasa.com/blog/capital-gains-tax-rsu-shares) .


## US-listed vs Indian-listed RSUs


The vesting-day treatment is the same wherever your employer is listed. The sale side is different.


Foreign-listed shares (for example, US) Indian-listed shares


Long-term holding period More than 24 months More than 12 months


Long-term rate 12.5%, no exemption 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh


Short-term rate Your slab rate 20%


Exchange rate conversion Yes No


Schedule FA reporting Yes No


Read[US-listed vs Indian-listed RSUs](https://paasa.com/blog/us-listed-vs-indian-listed-rsus-tax) for the full comparison.


## What your employer does not cover


Your employer's responsibility ends with TDS on the perquisite. Two things routinely fall outside it.


### 1. Advance tax


Capital gains on foreign shares and foreign dividends have no Indian TDS. Employers also sometimes withhold at a flat rate that is lower than your actual marginal rate once surcharge is counted.


If your tax due for the year, after TDS, is ₹10,000 or more, you must pay advance tax in four instalments (15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March). Falling short leads to interest under sections 424 and 425 (earlier 234B and 234C).


Read[advance tax for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/advance-tax-rsu-holders) for how to estimate each instalment.


### 2. Dividends


If you keep the shares and the company pays dividends, the US withholds 25% at source for Indian residents who have a valid W-8BEN on file. India then taxes the gross dividend at your slab rate as income from other sources.


You can claim the US tax as a foreign tax credit by filing Form 44 (Form 67 for FY 2025-26 and earlier). Read[how dividend income from RSU shares is taxed](https://paasa.com/blog/dividend-income-from-rsu-shares-taxed) and[W-8BEN for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/w-8ben-rsu-holders) .


## Where RSUs go in your tax return


RSU holders with foreign shares cannot use ITR-1. The table follows the current ITR-2 layout.


What Where it goes When it applies


Perquisite at vesting Schedule S (salary), matching Form 130 Every year shares vest


Sale of shares, including the sell-to-cover lot Schedule CG Every year you sell


Foreign shares and brokerage account Schedule FA Every year you hold them as an ordinary resident, on a calendar-year basis


Foreign dividends and gains taxed abroad Schedule FSI and Schedule TR, plus Form 44 When you claim foreign tax credit


Assets and liabilities Schedule AL When total income exceeds ₹1 crore


Schedule FA is mandatory even in a year with no vest, no sale and no dividend. Read[ITR for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/itr-for-rsu-holders) and[Schedule FA for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/schedule-fa-rsu-holders) for the line-by-line detail.


## How residential status changes the picture


Status Perquisite at vesting Gain on selling foreign shares Schedule FA


Resident and ordinarily resident (ROR) Fully taxable Taxable Required


Resident but not ordinarily resident (RNOR) Taxable for the part earned through work in India Not taxable if received outside India Not required


Non-resident (NR) Taxable for the part earned through work in India Not taxable in India Not required


If you worked in more than one country during the vesting period, the perquisite is split by the days worked in each. Read[are RSU vesting events taxable during RNOR](https://paasa.com/blog/are-rsu-vesting-events-taxable-during-rnor) and[RSU taxation across multiple countries](https://paasa.com/blog/rsu-taxation-multiple-countries-pro-rata) .


## Old vs new tax regime in an RSU year


The RSU perquisite is taxed as salary under both regimes, and the capital gains rates are the same in both. The difference lies in the slabs, the deductions and the top surcharge.


- **New regime (the default):** lower slab rates, few deductions, and surcharge capped at 25%. The highest rate on a vest is 39%.
- **Old regime:** deductions such as 80C and home loan interest remain, but surcharge rises to 37% above ₹5 crore. The highest rate on a vest is 42.74%.


Run both before you file, because a big vest year can change the answer from the year before.


**Filing for FY 2025-26?** Income up to 31 March 2026 is still governed by the Income-tax Act, 1961. Use the old numbers: section 17(2)(vi) for the perquisite, section 49(2AA) for cost of acquisition, section 192 for TDS, Rule 115 for the exchange rate and Form 67 for foreign tax credit. The rules themselves did not change. See our[old-to-new section mapping](https://paasa.com/blog/income-tax-act-2025-old-to-new-mapping) .


## Common mistakes


- **Assuming tax is due only on sale.** The larger tax bill arrives at vesting, before any cash does.
- **Using the grant price or the sale price as cost.** Your cost is the rupee value taxed at vesting.
- **Using the wrong exchange rate.** Both the perquisite and the sale use SBI's TTBR on the last day of the previous month, not the rate on the day or your bank's rate.
- **Applying the ₹1.25 lakh exemption or the 12-month rule.** Both belong to Indian listed equity.
- **Skipping Schedule FA in a quiet year.** Holding the shares is enough to trigger it.
- **Ignoring advance tax.** TDS at vesting rarely covers surcharge, dividends and capital gains.
